summary: Trinity County lookout on Mad River Rock, built 1935 to replace Hetten Peak lookout; dismantled; stair and trail remnants reported.

facts.design: Lookout on top of the rock, reached by 230 steps; materials swung up by high line
facts.status_note: Kemnow page marks it removed, with no date; a trip report says it was dismantled

visit.trail_note: Trip report describes a technically difficult climb and old stair remnants on the north side; no visitor route is documented

events.note: Forest Service announced it would abandon the Hetten Peak lookout in favor of a new lookout on Mad River Rock
Oakland Tribune feature describes the road, high line and 230 steps used to build the lookout

evidence.supports: Trinity County location and elevation of the rock
evidence.quote: its top reaching an elevation of 4300 feet above sea level.

evidence.supports: Mad River Rock lies on Mad River Ridge
evidence.quote: lying on Mad River Ridge between the valley of that name and the Van Dusen River Valley.

evidence.supports: July 1934: road and new lookout planned; Hetten Peak lookout to be abandoned
evidence.quote: Forest service is now building a new road to Mad River Rock where they will build a new lookout. Hetten Peak lookout will be abandoned and Mad River Rock will take its place.

evidence.supports: Nearest highway was eight miles away
evidence.quote: It was ONLY eight miles to the nearest highway.

evidence.supports: Superintendent given eight days for the road
evidence.quote: Kaufmann was told to build a road to the foot of the rock and do it all in eight days.

evidence.supports: CCC crew and bulldozer built the road in ten days
evidence.quote: Using a bulldozer, powder and a fleet of trucks and a crew of husky CCC youths the superintendent constructed the road in ten days.

evidence.supports: High line swung lumber and materials to the top of the rock
evidence.quote: Boys climbed the rock, a high line was constructed and lumber and other materials were swung to the top of the rock.
Steps? Yes, Sir. 230 of them and its quite a chore to climb them.

evidence.supports: Trip report: Mad River Rock lies within Six Rivers National Forest
evidence.quote: Six Rivers National Forest (same as Black Lassic, Mad River Rock and the other

evidence.supports: A forest lookout once stood atop the rock and has been dismantled
evidence.quote: A forest lookout once stood atop Mad River Rock, but it has long since been dismantled.

evidence.supports: Remains of an old trail on the north side and wooden stairs
evidence.quote: remains of an old trail built on its northern aspect

evidence.supports: Remains of wooden stairs at the end of the old trail
Writer suggests the rock may be the most technically difficult P1K in the state
evidence.quote: the most technically difficult P1K in the state

notes_for_editor: Two sources: Kemnow's page with 1934 and 1935 newspaper quotes, and a trip report. The 1935 Oakland Tribune article names a superintendent, Kaufmann; no other source found for him. No removal date found. A concrete block on a summit in the same trip report belongs to a different peak in the Lassic area, so it is excluded. The trip report also appears at peak_5,640ft_n3_1.html with identical text; signal_n3_1 is cited. A 1936 Humboldt Times clipping about a 'fire lookout at Mad River' appeared only in a search snippet and is unverified; not cited. The article's '1934 road' and '1935 built' dates come from one feature and are not corroborated. Record agency was null; the trip report's Six Rivers NF statement is used for facts.agency.
